reviewer: u4a-A — adversarial refutation pass, blind to the second reviewer

flags.detail: The keyed mechanism is the co-scheduling model VMware abandoned, and the stem is built on precisely the case that model does not cover. Option A (and the explanation) say the 16-vCPU VM 'waits until enough physical cores are free' because its vCPUs 'must progress together within a bounded skew'. That is strict co-scheduling (ESX 2.x); ESX 3 replaced it with relaxed co-scheduling, under which only vCPUs that have lagged past the skew threshold must be co-started, and — decisively here — a descheduled idle vCPU is counted as making progress and accumulates no skew at all (VMware, 'The CPU Scheduler in VMware ESX 4', whitepaper). The stem stipulates that only four threads are ever busy and guest CPU utilisation stays low, i.e. twelve idle vCPUs, which is exactly the workload relaxed co-scheduling was designed to stop penalising. So the question asserts a co-start stall in the one scenario where ESXi does not impose one. The observed symptom is real and right-sizing is real guidance, but the causes for a mostly-idle wide VM are per-vCPU scheduling and timer overhead raising %RDY, the VM exceeding a NUMA node's width so memory access goes remote, and guests that idle-poll rather than halt. Fix one of two ways: (a) change the stem so the guest actually keeps most of its 16 vCPUs busy (drop the 'never more than four threads busy / utilisation stays low' clause), which makes co-scheduling the honest explanation; or (b) keep the stem and reword option A and the explanation to attribute the loss to scheduling overhead, NUMA width and %RDY rather than to mandatory co-starting of all vCPUs. Option A is still the least-bad of the four as written, so this is a rationale defect, not a wrong key.
flags.suggested: Keep key A, but rewrite the stem to have most vCPUs busy, or rewrite A as: 'Every vCPU must still be scheduled and accounted for, and a VM wider than a NUMA node loses memory locality, so on a contended host the oversized VM accumulates CPU ready time and remote memory access that the 4-vCPU configuration avoided.'

flags.detail: The keyed option A overstates itself into something false as of 2026: 'nothing is charged while no requests are being served, so there is no provisioned instance count at all'. Every mainstream FaaS platform has shipped an opt-in always-warm tier that is exactly a provisioned instance count billed while idle — AWS Lambda Provisioned Concurrency (GA Dec 2019; AWS docs state you are billed for the configured provisioned concurrency whether or not it serves a request), Azure Functions Premium plan always-ready/pre-warmed instances, and Cloud Run/Cloud Functions min-instances. A is still clearly the best of the four (B and D are simply false, and C is false because mainstream PaaS has autoscaled for years, as the explanation itself says), so this is not a wrong key — but as written the option teaches an absolute that a candidate will meet contradicted in practice.
flags.suggested: Reword A to scope the claim to the default model: 'Capacity is allocated per invocation and, in the default on-demand model, nothing is charged while no requests are being served, so there is no baseline instance count to provision.' Optionally add a clause to the explanation noting opt-in provisioned-concurrency tiers as the exception.

flags.detail: Duplicate of GEN-T2U4-014 on the discriminating fact, the trap, and even the explanation's wording. Both turn on the single NIST SP 800-145 sentence that private cloud is defined by exclusive use by one organisation and 'may be owned, managed, and operated by the organization, a third party, or some combination of them, and it may exist on or off premises'; both bait the same misreading that vendor-owned and off-premises implies public cloud; both explanations state that location/ownership is not part of the definition. GEN-T2U4-006 is the weaker of the pair — bare definition recall — while GEN-T2U4-014 makes the candidate apply it to a scenario, so 014 should be kept. (They sit under different sub-topic tags, 'NIST cloud architecture' vs 'Deployment and service models', which is presumably how two lesson batches both landed on it.)
flags.suggested: Keep GEN-T2U4-014 and re-point GEN-T2U4-006 at an untested part of the deployment-model taxonomy — e.g. the community cloud definition (shared by organisations with common concerns such as mission, security requirements, policy or compliance considerations), which no other question in this batch touches, or the public cloud definition's 'provisioned for open use by the general public' clause.

notes: Strong batch: I attacked all 35 and could not break the key on any of them. Every NIST-derived item (001, 002, 006, 008, 009, 010, 014) matches SP 800-145 / SP 500-292 verbatim, the HPA arithmetic in 020 is correct against the documented ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / desiredMetric) formula and clears the 0.1 tolerance, and the virtualisation block (027-035) is accurate on Popek-Goldberg, VMCS/VMCB non-root operation, two-dimensional EPT walks, balloon-vs-TPS-vs-compression-vs-host-swap, SR-IOV VFs vs PCI passthrough vs virtio, qcow2 backing files and UNMAP/TRIM. Provider-specific leakage, the risk I attacked hardest, is well controlled: the two provider-flavoured items name their platform (031 says vSphere, 033 says KVM/qemu-img) and the FaaS items (015, 017) rest on behaviour common to Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Run rather than to one vendor. The three findings are one rationale defect worth fixing (031), one absolute that modern always-warm tiers contradict (012), and one redundant pair (006/014); none is a wrong key.
